questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention the difference between Primary and Secondary Evoked potential?
questions.modelAnswer:
• Primary Evoked Potential: Localized.
• Secondary Evoked Potential: Diffuse.
questions.explanation: Primary evoked potential is localized to a specific sensory projection area, while secondary evoked potential is diffuse and recorded from wide cortical areas.
questions.keyConcept: Difference between Primary and Secondary Evoked potential

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention the significance of EEG recorded from the scalp?
questions.modelAnswer: • Measure of summation of post-synaptic potentials (PSPs) of neurons in the cerebral cortex.
questions.explanation: The electroencephalogram (EEG) recorded from the scalp reflects the summation of post-synaptic potentials (both excitatory and inhibitory) of underlying cortical neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Significance of EEG recorded from scalp

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Detect EEG wave of adult awake relaxed person with eye closed, Mention it's cause?
questions.modelAnswer:
Wave:
• Alpha wave

Cause:
• Activity of nonspecific thalamic nuclei.
questions.explanation: Alpha waves are recorded in an adult who is awake, relaxed, and has their eyes closed. They are generated by the activity of nonspecific thalamic nuclei (thalamocortical pacemaker system).
questions.keyConcept: EEG wave of adult awake relaxed person with eyes closed and its cause

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention site of recording of Beta wave and it's significance?
questions.modelAnswer:
Site of Recording:
• Frontal and Parietal regions

Significance:
• Brain activity (alertness, active thinking, or attention)
questions.explanation: Beta waves are recorded from frontal and parietal regions during active mental work, alert state, or attention (representing desynchronization of alpha rhythm).
questions.keyConcept: Site of recording and significance of Beta wave

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention the wave of Hyper arousal and it's site?
questions.modelAnswer:
Wave:
• Gamma wave

Site:
• All cortical areas
questions.explanation: Gamma waves are recorded from all cortical areas during states of hyper-arousal, higher cognitive processing, or complex mental activity.
questions.keyConcept: Wave and site of hyper arousal

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which EEG wave recorded in light sleep/Deep sleep?
questions.modelAnswer:
• Light sleep: Theta wave
• Deep sleep: Delta wave
questions.explanation: Theta waves are recorded during light sleep (stage 1 & 2), whereas delta waves are recorded during deep sleep (stage 3 & 4/slow-wave sleep).
questions.keyConcept: EEG waves in light sleep vs deep sleep

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.modelAnswer: • Regular Alpha rhythm is replaced by fast, irregular, low-voltage beta rhythm (alert/active state).
questions.explanation: Desynchronization (or alpha block) is the replacement of the synchronous, regular alpha rhythm with the asynchronous, fast, low-voltage beta rhythm when the eyes are opened or during active mental effort.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.modelAnswer:
| Feature | NREM Sleep | REM (Paradoxical) Sleep |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Eye Movements** | No REM; eyes up & miosed | Rapid Eye Movements (REM) |
| **Muscle Tone** | Slightly inhibited | Marked decrease (strong inhibition) |
| **Body Movement** | Sleep walking/talking present | Large movements absent; small twitches |
| **Autonomics** | ↓ Pulse, BP, Resp, BMR (Parasympathetic) | ↑/Irregular Pulse, BP, Resp (Sympathetic) |
| **Dreaming** | None (or not remembered) | Active dreams (remembered) |
| **Arousal** | Easy (Low threshold) | Difficult (High threshold) |
| **Growth Hormone** | Increased | Decreased |
| **Other Signs** | Erection & teeth grinding absent | Erection & teeth grinding present |
questions.explanation: Comparison between Non-Rapid Eye Movement (NREM) and Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep across major physiological features including eye movement, muscle tone, autonomic changes, and dreams.
questions.keyConcept: Comparison between REM and NREM sleep

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention type of sleep in which person is difficult to be aroused and why?
questions.modelAnswer:
Type of Sleep:
• REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep

Why:
• The threshold of arousal is high (strong inhibition of sensory inputs and muscle tone).
questions.explanation: A person is more difficult to arouse during REM (paradoxical) sleep because the arousal threshold is high due to marked descending inhibition of sensory transmission and motor pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Type of sleep with high arousal threshold and explanation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is EEG change recorded in REM ?
questions.modelAnswer:
• Rapid, irregular, low-voltage Beta-wave-like activity (desynchronized beta rhythm).
• This is similar to the alert state, which is why REM is called Paradoxical sleep.
questions.explanation: During REM sleep, the EEG shows a desynchronized pattern of rapid, irregular, low-voltage beta-like activity similar to an awake/alert state, earning it the name paradoxical sleep.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.modelAnswer: • Indicates marked brain activity (such as active dreaming and memory consolidation) while the person is asleep.
questions.explanation: Paradoxical sleep is significant because it indicates high levels of cortical metabolic and neuronal activity (including active dreaming and dreaming recall) in the presence of sleep.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.modelAnswer:
• REM Center: Reticular Formation (RF) in the upper part of the brain stem (pons).
• NREM Center: Anterior Hypothalamus and adjacent basal forebrain area.
questions.explanation: REM sleep is controlled primarily by cholinergic nuclei in the pontine reticular formation, whereas NREM sleep is driven by GABAergic/galaninergic neurons in the anterior hypothalamus (preoptic area) and basal forebrain.
questions.keyConcept: Brain centers regulating REM and NREM sleep

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention the site which synchronizes sleep/wakefulness rhythm with dark light cycle?
questions.explanation: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus acts as the master circadian pacemaker, synchronizing the sleep-wake cycle with the external 24-hour light-dark cycle via inputs from the retinohypothalamic tract.
questions.keyConcept: Site synchronizing sleep/wakefulness rhythm with light-dark cycle

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention the chemical transmitter which is switch between sleep and wakefulness?
questions.explanation: Orexin (hypocretin), produced by lateral hypothalamic neurons, acts as the key chemical transmitter switch that stabilizes wakefulness and prevents inappropriate transitions between sleep and waking states.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical transmitter acting as sleep-wake switch

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention 3 chemical substances increase in wakefulness?
questions.explanation: Wakefulness is promoted by neurotransmitters including norepinephrine (from locus coeruleus), serotonin (from raphe nuclei), and histamine (from tuberomammillary nucleus).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention the chemical transmitter which increases in REM ?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine levels increase significantly in the pons and cortex during REM sleep, driving the desynchronization of the EEG.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical transmitter increased in REM sleep

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention 2 chemical transmitters decreased in Wakefulness?
questions.modelAnswer:
• Acetylcholine (in certain sleep-promoting pathways)
• GABA (Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid)
questions.explanation: Wakefulness is characterized by low activity of sleep-promoting GABAergic neurotransmission and certain quiet cholinergic states, though wakefulness generally relies on amine pathways.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mention one transmitter increased and the other decreased in NREM?
questions.explanation: NREM sleep is initiated and maintained by increased GABA levels (which inhibit the arousal centers) and decreased histamine levels (reducing arousal signaling).
questions.keyConcept: Neurotransmitters increased and decreased in NREM sleep
